claims.text: TiH2 can function as an oxygen getter in the HfNbTaTiZr precursor blend.
Synchronizing TaH0.5 and NbH decomposition with HfH2, TiH2, and ZrH2 decomposition will promote formation of the target alloy.
TaH0.5 and NbH begin decomposing at approximately 600–700 K.
A heating rate of 10 K min⁻¹ is an appropriate ramp for the proposed process.
The sintering atmosphere should be high-purity Ar containing less than 10 ppm O2.
A temperature above 1400 K is sufficient for homogenization of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Rapid quenching can reproduce additive-manufacturing cooling rates of 10⁴–10⁶ K⁻¹.
TiH2 reacts with trace oxygen during heating to produce TiO2.
The generated TiO2 acts as an oxygen sink and inhibits nucleation of alpha-Ti and other alpha-HCP phases.
Hydride decomposition releases hydrogen and leaves reactive metal species that drive alloying.
Removing residual oxygen prevents oxygen-induced stabilization of alpha-HCP phases in HfNbTaTiZr.
Rapid cooling suppresses diffusion needed for alpha-phase precipitation.
Rapid quenching traps a metastable single-phase beta-BCC structure.
The proposed regime will produce an alloy with greater than 99% relative density.
The rapidly quenched alloy will have a grain size of 10–20 µm.
The final alloy will be free of alpha-HCP and alpha-Ti phases.
Conventional sintering with Ti powder or no getter produces dual BCC or alpha-HCP structures, significant porosity, and alpha-Ti precipitates because of oxygen contamination.
Successful oxygen control requires TiH2 activation not to lag significantly behind TaH0.5 and NbH decomposition.
In-situ synchrotron XRD during heating can track phase evolution through temperature-dependent diffraction peaks.
The target equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr composition contains approximately 20 at.% each of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts in-situ formation and XRD detection of TiO2 but also describes the final microstructure as single-phase beta-BCC. Persistent TiO2 would constitute an additional phase unless it is removed or remains below detection, neither of which is specified.
The hypothesis calls alpha-Ti an intermetallic, whereas the experiment identifies alpha-Ti as an HCP phase. Alpha-Ti is an elemental HCP allotrope rather than an intermetallic compound.
